nameStory: The flat pillbug gets its name from its extremely flattened body shape, which sets it apart from the familiar rounded pill bugs that roll into perfect balls. While most pillbugs are dome-shaped like tiny armadillos, this species looks like it's been gently pressed flat, earning it the descriptive 'flat' designation.
description: The flat pillbug is a small terrestrial crustacean that looks like a miniature gray or brownish oval disk with legs. Unlike the common pillbugs you might find in your garden, this species has a distinctly flattened, almost pancake-like body that rarely exceeds half an inch in length. It's part of the diverse world of isopods - the same group that includes both pillbugs and their marine cousins like sea lice. **Note: This species is extremely rare in New England with only one recorded observation, so information should be considered preliminary.**

idTips.label: Flattened Body Shape
idTips.description: The body is remarkably flat and wide, feeling almost paper-thin compared to common pillbugs when gently pressed - like comparing a coin to a marble

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Very small, typically 4-6mm long, about the size of a large grain of rice or small peppercorn

idTips.label: Color Pattern
idTips.description: Grayish-brown to dark brown coloration, often with a mottled or slightly marbled appearance across the segments

idTips.label: Rolling Ability
idTips.description: Cannot roll into a complete ball like common pillbugs - the flat body prevents this defensive behavior

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Smooth, hard exoskeleton with subtle segmentation visible as faint lines across the flattened back

habitat: **Uncertain due to limited data** - Likely found in specialized microhabitats such as under very flat stones, in rock crevices, or between layers of decaying bark where the flattened body shape provides an advantage. May prefer slightly drier conditions than common pillbugs, possibly in sandy or rocky soils with good drainage.

seasonality.spring: **Data limited** - Most likely to be found as temperatures warm and individuals become more active under stones and debris.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when populations would be most detectable, though they remain hidden in narrow crevices during hot days.
seasonality.fall: May still be active in protected microhabitats, potentially preparing for winter dormancy.
seasonality.winter: Likely dormant in deep crevices or protected spaces, essentially undetectable to casual observation.

funFact: This tiny crustacean has evolved its pancake-flat body to live in spaces so narrow that most other land crustaceans can't even fit - it's like nature's version of a living credit card that can squeeze into gaps barely thicker than a piece of cardboard!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with very young common pillbugs, but the flat pillbug maintains its distinctly flattened shape even as an adult, while young pillbugs are simply smaller versions of the rounded adults. Remember: if it looks like it was run over by a tiny steamroller, it's probably a flat pillbug!
contextualKnowledge: **Important note**: This species is extremely rare in New England with only one recorded observation in our dataset. Any sighting would be scientifically significant and should be documented with photos and location data. The extreme rarity means that identification should be approached with caution and expert verification is recommended.
compareHints: **Limited comparison data available** - As the only Ancinus species in our New England dataset, it's most easily compared to other small isopods by its distinctive flattened profile. Unlike members of other pillbug families, flat pillbugs cannot roll into balls and have proportionally wider, more compressed bodies relative to their length.
